Family Health

Ovarian cancer symptoms: seven changes to discuss and how to seek assessment

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Ovarian cancer can cause symptoms that overlap with common digestive, urinary and gynecologic conditions. A symptom list cannot tell you whether cancer is present, but a new pattern that persists or keeps returning deserves attention. Knowing what to describe and how to arrange follow-up can help you get an appropriate assessment.

Why these symptoms can be overlooked

Early changes may be mild or resemble irritable bowel symptoms, a urinary infection or ordinary menstrual discomfort. Most people with an episode of bloating or back pain do not have ovarian cancer, but repeatedly attributing an unexplained change to a familiar problem can delay further investigation.

A cancer can also be present without a clear early warning. There is no symptom checklist that reliably identifies every early case. Pay attention to changes from your usual pattern, while recognizing that an instinct that something is different is a reason to seek assessment: not a diagnosis.

Earlier detection generally offers a better outlook. As context, US SEER data for 2016–2022 report five-year relative survival of 91.9% for localized ovarian cancer and about 22% of cases diagnosed at that stage. These population figures do not predict an individual outcome or mean that someone is to blame when a diagnosis is later.

The American Cancer Society’s 2026 US lifetime-risk estimate is about 1 in 91. Risk varies between individuals and populations. Whether a symptom needs attention depends on the clinical situation, not on treating an average as personal reassurance.

1. Bloating or an abdomen that stays enlarged

Temporary bloating around a period or after certain foods is common. A more persistent change may be noticeable because a waistband becomes tight, buttons or a zip are harder to fasten, or the abdomen seems enlarged in a way that does not settle as usual.

These are examples of how a change may be described, not a test for cancer. Tell the clinician whether the swelling comes and goes, is becoming more pronounced, or occurs alongside pain, eating difficulties or changes in weight.

One cause of abdominal swelling is ascites, a collection of fluid in the abdomen. In cancer, fluid can accumulate when the abdominal lining is affected or normal lymphatic drainage is disrupted. Ascites also has noncancerous causes, and ordinary bloating does not establish that fluid or cancer cells are present.

Significant or worsening swelling needs assessment. If it is accompanied by severe pain, persistent vomiting or difficulty breathing, seek prompt care rather than waiting to complete a symptom diary.

2. Abdominal or pelvic pain

Discomfort may feel like pressure, a persistent ache or cramping. Some people compare it with menstrual pain, but the location and sensation vary. There is no particular description that confirms ovarian cancer.

A growing mass can press on structures such as the bowel, bladder or nearby tissues. Other conditions can cause similar pain, including noncancerous ovarian problems, infection and digestive disorders. The pattern and associated symptoms help guide assessment.

Explain where the pain occurs, when it began, whether it is continuous and what makes it better or worse. Include its effect on sleep, movement or daily activities. Sudden severe pain or pain with faintness needs urgent attention, regardless of whether cancer is being considered.

3. Bowel changes or new urinary urgency

Changes in bowel habits can include constipation, diarrhoea or a pattern different from your usual one. A short-lived change after a meal or infection is different from a continuing unexplained problem, but you do not need to wait until it is severe to ask for advice.

Urinary changes may include needing to pass urine more often or feeling an urgent need to go. Some people also describe burning or a sense that the bladder has not emptied. These symptoms can have several causes; burning is particularly important to mention because infection and other urinary conditions need consideration.

Tell the clinician about bowel and bladder symptoms together, including any treatment already tried and whether it helped. If an assumed urinary or digestive problem does not improve as expected, arrange another review.

Inability to pass urine, or persistent vomiting with a swollen abdomen and inability to pass stool or gas, needs urgent assessment rather than more self-treatment.

4. Back or side pain that is unexplained

Back pain is very common and usually has an explanation other than cancer. A recent strain, posture or another musculoskeletal problem may account for it. Pain in the lower back or side should nevertheless be discussed if it is unexplained, continues or does not respond as expected to treatment.

Mention whether it occurs alongside bloating, pelvic discomfort, urinary symptoms or appetite changes. That combination can help the clinician decide which areas to investigate without assuming that every symptom has one cause.

The absence of an obvious injury does not prove cancer. Equally, a previous back problem should not prevent reassessment of a new or changing pattern.

5. Feeling full quickly or losing your appetite

A change may be noticeable when you feel full after much less food than usual, lose interest in eating or repeatedly feel uncomfortable after meals. Indigestion, nausea or vomiting may accompany it. Difficulty eating can contribute to unintentional weight loss.

These symptoms may be attributed initially to reflux or another digestive condition. That may be the correct explanation, but ongoing early fullness or appetite loss needs follow-up if treatment does not help.

Describe the change in concrete terms: whether portions have become smaller, meals are being skipped, weight is changing or you cannot keep food or fluids down. The aim is to explain the impact, not to diagnose the cause from the amount you can eat.

6. Changes in periods, bleeding or discharge

If you menstruate, report unexplained changes such as a missed period, heavier bleeding or spotting between periods. New or unusual discharge is also worth mentioning. These changes have many possible causes and should not all be assigned to an ovarian condition.

Any vaginal bleeding after menopause needs assessment, even if it happens only once or consists of a small amount of spotting. It does not usually mean ovarian cancer. Common explanations include thinning of the vaginal or uterine lining and polyps; the clinician also needs to consider more serious causes, including uterine cancer.

Bleeding after sex also deserves review. Tell the clinician whether bleeding is definitely vaginal or could be coming from the urinary tract or bowel, if you can tell. Uncertainty is itself useful to mention.

Heavy bleeding with faintness or severe pain needs urgent care. You do not need to wait for a routine cancer referral to have an acute problem assessed.

7. Pain during sex

Pain during sex is sometimes overlooked because it feels difficult to bring up. It can occur with ovarian cancer, but many other explanations are more common, including vaginal dryness, endometriosis, inflammation and involuntary tightening of pelvic-floor muscles.

Mention whether pain occurs at the vaginal entrance, deeper in the pelvis, during particular contact or afterwards. You can also say simply that sex has become painful if describing it in detail feels difficult.

Stop activity that hurts rather than pushing through it. Identifying the cause matters even when cancer is not involved, because treatment may improve both physical comfort and the distress surrounding intimacy.

Risk factors to discuss without treating them as a verdict

Tell the clinician about relatives with ovarian or breast cancer, particularly close relatives or younger diagnoses. A personal or family history of certain breast, colorectal or uterine cancers may point to an inherited cancer syndrome. A vague history of any gynecologic problem is not the same as a confirmed cancer risk.

Inherited pathogenic variants in BRCA1 or BRCA2 are important examples. Other syndromes can also matter. If a genetic test has already been done, bring the actual result when possible rather than relying on a remembered abbreviation.

Endometriosis, having never had a full-term pregnancy and higher body weight are associated with risk in some settings, with differences between tumour types. These associations do not identify the cause of an individual illness and should not be used to blame someone for their reproductive history or body size.

Menopausal hormone therapy can also affect risk and belongs in the medication history. Discuss the overall benefits and risks with the prescriber; do not stop a prescribed treatment solely because of a symptom article.

The relationship with fertility treatment needs nuance. ASRM’s 2024 guideline describes a possible small increase in ovarian-cancer risk, while explaining the difficulty of separating treatment from underlying infertility, endometriosis and reproductive history. It is inaccurate to treat every fertility medicine as a proven direct cause.

Someone with no recognized risk factor can still need investigation. Conversely, a risk factor does not mean that a current symptom is cancer. Symptoms and risk information should be considered together by the clinician.

How an assessment may proceed

A clinician asks about the changes, examines the abdomen and may recommend a pelvic examination. Examination can identify tenderness, swelling or a mass, but it cannot reliably exclude ovarian cancer. The purpose of any intimate examination should be explained, and you can ask for it to stop.

An ultrasound may be performed through the abdomen or with a probe placed in the vagina. It provides images of the ovaries and nearby structures and helps assess a suspected mass. A transvaginal scan should be discussed with you, including what to expect and any concerns you have.

A CA-125 blood test measures a marker that can be elevated in ovarian cancer. It can also rise for benign reasons, and some cancers do not raise it. A single positive or negative result is therefore not a complete diagnosis.

Concerning findings may lead to a gynecologic oncology team, CT imaging or other investigations. Tissue examination establishes the type of a suspected tumour. The specialist decides whether a sample should come from surgery or another procedure; not every ovarian mass follows the same biopsy route.

Cervical screening, including a Pap test, does not screen the ovaries. A reassuring cervical result should not be used to dismiss ongoing abdominal or pelvic symptoms.

Why a normal screening history is not enough

For people without symptoms at average risk, routine ovarian screening with CA-125 or ultrasound has not been shown to reduce deaths and can lead to false positives and unnecessary procedures. That is different from ordering tests to investigate a symptom.

If you have a strong inherited risk, care should be planned separately with an appropriate specialist. Neither a routine annual scan nor a normal examination should be assumed to remove that risk.

A normal initial scan or blood result may be reassuring, but continuing symptoms still deserve a plan. Ask what other causes will be investigated and when to return if the problem does not settle.

Self-advocacy can help, but diagnosis is not your responsibility

Self-advocacy means making your concerns, preferences and practical needs known. It can help the healthcare team understand what matters to you and help you participate in decisions. It does not mean that you have to identify cancer yourself or persuade someone using medical terminology.

Speaking up can be difficult when you are anxious, depressed, naturally reserved or unfamiliar with the healthcare system. Differences in age, education or professional status can also make an appointment feel intimidating.

Previous experiences of discrimination or disbelief related to gender, race, identity, disability or income may make trust harder. Problems obtaining appointments, paying for care or communicating in the available language can add to the burden.

These are real barriers, not evidence that you are failing to look after yourself. A clinician remains responsible for listening, assessing and arranging appropriate follow-up. A late diagnosis is not proof that a patient was insufficiently assertive.

Support with communication can make it easier to ask for help earlier, understand options and coordinate with people around you. Those are useful goals without promising that assertiveness will determine a cancer outcome.

Prepare a short record and a few clear questions

Write down when each important change began, how often it occurs, whether it is getting worse and how it affects eating, sleep or daily activities. Include treatments already tried and their effect. A short record is enough; do not delay an appointment while trying to produce a perfect diary.

Put new symptoms near the top of your notes, especially when you already live with a digestive or urinary condition. Explain what is different from your usual pattern. Include relevant medicines, past cancer diagnoses and family or genetic history.

Prepare the questions you most want answered. For example: What are the possible causes? Is ovarian cancer among the conditions being considered? What would each test show? What happens if the result is normal but I still feel unwell?

Ask where tests will take place, whether a referral is needed and how costs or insurance coverage can be clarified in your healthcare system. Reliable health information can help you understand the discussion without requiring you to choose every investigation yourself.

You can keep the notes on paper or a phone and refer to them during the visit. Tell the clinician if anxiety makes it hard to remember information, and ask for the next steps in writing when that would help.

Bring support and ask for clarification or referral

A trusted friend or family member may help you remember questions, take notes or describe changes they have noticed, if you want them involved. Someone who has experienced cancer may offer practical support, but their diagnosis or treatment cannot establish what your symptoms mean.

You can ask for an interpreter, accessible information, a support person or other communication help. Explain how you prefer information to be given and ask the clinician to pause when something is unclear.

If you feel a concern has been minimized, state it specifically: the symptom is new, it has lasted this long, and the current explanation has not resolved it. Ask what would justify further testing or specialist referral and what the plan is if it continues.

A respectful, direct conversation can help, but you do not have to be perfectly calm or phrase a request flawlessly to deserve care. If trust has broken down or concerns remain unanswered, requesting another opinion or a different clinician is reasonable.

Changing clinicians may take time and may not be easy. While arranging it, keep existing follow-up and know how to obtain urgent care if symptoms worsen. The aim is continuity and a clear assessment, not having to start from the beginning repeatedly.

Leave with a follow-up plan

Before the appointment ends, establish when results are expected, who will explain them and whom to contact if they do not arrive. Ask whether you need to book the next visit yourself. Do not assume that silence always means a normal result.

Find out which changes should trigger a quicker review and what to do outside normal clinic hours. If the symptoms persist, worsen or become more frequent, return even if the first tests were reassuring.

The process can feel frightening while the cause remains uncertain. Practical support and a clinician who explains the next step can help. You deserve assessment of ongoing bloating, pain, eating difficulties, bowel or urinary changes, unusual bleeding or painful sex without having to prove a diagnosis first.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS guidance recommends review of persistent symptoms and reassessment when symptoms do not settle, worsen or become more frequent. Postmenopausal bleeding has several possible causes and should be checked even after a single episode.

The National Cancer Institute encourages preparing questions and discussing communication needs. ASRM advises a nuanced discussion of fertility-treatment evidence rather than treating all medicines as a proven cause of ovarian cancer.

How BeMama can help

BeMama offers general education to help you prepare questions and describe changes clearly. You can use this article to organize a brief symptom history and ask for a follow-up plan. BeMama cannot decide which tests you need or diagnose cancer from symptoms.

When to seek help

Seek prompt care for sudden severe pain, faintness, heavy bleeding, persistent vomiting, a swollen abdomen with inability to pass stool or gas, inability to pass urine or breathing difficulty. Arrange assessment for persistent nonurgent changes and any bleeding after menopause.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Look for persistent or recurring changes from your normal pattern; symptoms alone do not confirm cancer.
  • The seven symptom areas include bloating, pelvic pain, bowel or urinary changes, back pain, appetite changes, bleeding and pain during sex.
  • Postmenopausal bleeding needs assessment even once, but usually has another explanation besides ovarian cancer.
  • CA-125, ultrasound and examination have limits. Ask for follow-up if symptoms continue.
  • Notes, support people and clear questions can help; a delayed diagnosis is not the patient’s fault.

Frequently asked questions

Does bloating after a meal mean ovarian cancer?

Usually it has another explanation. A new persistent or recurring change, especially with other symptoms or increasing abdominal size, should be discussed with a clinician.

Should I wait until I have several symptoms?

No. One persistent or concerning change can be enough to seek advice. Severe pain, persistent vomiting, faintness or heavy bleeding needs prompt care.

Does postmenopausal bleeding usually mean ovarian cancer?

No. Several noncancerous conditions are common causes, but any bleeding after menopause needs assessment to identify the cause and exclude serious disease.

Can a normal CA-125 test or Pap test rule it out?

No. CA-125 does not detect every ovarian cancer, and a Pap test assesses the cervix rather than the ovaries. Follow up symptoms that continue.

Did fertility treatment cause my symptoms or cancer risk?

Symptoms need their own assessment. Research on fertility treatment and ovarian cancer is complex; ASRM describes a possible small association that is difficult to separate from underlying factors. Discuss your specific history with the clinician.

What can I say if I feel dismissed?

Explain what is new, how long it has continued and how it affects you. Ask what further assessment or referral would be appropriate and when to return. You may also seek another opinion.

What if I find it hard to speak during an appointment?

Bring short notes, ask for communication support or bring a trusted person if you wish. You should not need perfect language or confidence to receive appropriate care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
